3.text: wards. He was passing between the ice-fields and the shore, and went as

4.text: far as Chaun Bay. There he carried on traffic with the Chukchee, and then

6.text: In 1649 a public-service man of the Yakutsk fortress, Timothy Bulgakoff,

7.text: was sent to the Kolyma. He left the mouth of the Lena, and reached the

8.text: Omoloi River. There be staid for four weeks, because of the ice and the un-

9.text: favorable weather. After that he went farther, but could not reach the

10.text: Kolyma: so he turned back toward the mouth of the Lena. On the way

11.text: he met eight galiots (galleys) full of the Czar’s serving-men, traders and ad-

12.text: venturers, who also were waiting for a favorable wind. At last the south

13.text: wind cleared off the ice. So they joined forces and set off for the open sea.

14.text: At sea they met four other ships going from the Kolyma. Near the Bay

15.text: of Khroma all of them were caught in the ice. The ships were crushed; but

16.text: the people escaped on ice-floes, and after many hardships succeeded in landing

17.text: at the mouth of the Indighirka River.²

18.text: This lively movement of the Russians in the Arctic waters of eastern

19.text: Siberia presents a strange contrast to their modern inactivity. The Russian

20.text: creoles, the descendants of the first conquerors, forgot the art of constructing

21.text: ships and their use. One of the reasons of this was that those ships were

22.text: too helpless and unwieldy to be used for travel among the ice of the Arctic

23.text: Ocean, and almost every other voyage ended in ruin.

24.text: The ships used by the Cossacks were called “cocha” (коча, pl. кочи).

25.text: They were large and uncouth, made of wooden planks tied together with

26.text: split willow-roots. These were fastened in the drill-holes with wooden pins.

27.text: Sphagnum was used for caulking. A heavy stone served for an anchor.

28.text: The sails were made, for the most part, of curried reindeer-skins sewed to-

29.text: gether. Up to the present time the small river-boats of the Kolyma River

30.text: have been built in the same way by Russian creoles and by the Yukaghir

31.text: of the Upper Kolyma. By the way, the Yukaghir far surpass the Russians at

32.text: present in their skill in making boats, and their boats are eagerly bought by

33.text: Russians in Sredne-Kolymsk and Nishne-Kolymsk, though there cannot be the

34.text: slightest doubt that the Yukaghir learned the art of boat-making from the Russians.

35.text: The art of constructing those clumsy ships was almost lost as early as

36.text: the beginning of the eighteenth century. Thus, in one of the reports of the

37.text: first years of the eighteenth century, the Cossacks say, “Our ships are small,

38.text: and the sails weak. We are unable to make larger ships, as in former times.”

39.text: For the next half-century we have only one historical date, 1690. In

40.text: this year the Cossack officer Basile Kusnetzov went on an expedition to the

41.text: country of the Koryak, and then to the country of the Chukchee. There

42.text: he was murdered by the Chukchee, together with all his followers.³
